I've been farming this land since I was a young man. My father grew wheat and maize on this same plot, and his father before him. The soil here on the North China Plain is good flat ground — there's no reason to do anything clever. I know what the ground wants and I know what the grain stations will buy.

My land is about 8 mu total. I'll plant winter wheat this autumn on all of it, then follow with summer maize on the same ground after harvest, like always. That's two crops a year. That's how you make ends meet around here.

For wheat, I'll use the improved seed from the county seed station — "矮抗58" type, it's what my neighbors use and yields are reliable. I'll rotary till before sowing, put down base fertilizer, then top-dress at jointing. I'll irrigate three times: once for winter protection in November, once at jointing, once at grain filling. I know the government says to cut to one or two waterings to save groundwater, but three is what the wheat needs to look right and I'm not willing to risk the yield. I'll spray twice for aphids and rust, once more for weeds early on.

For maize, I'll go straight in after wheat harvest — no time to lose in June. Hybrid seed, no tilling, just direct seeding into the stubble. Rain is more reliable in summer so I'll only need to water twice if there's a dry spell. Maize needs more nitrogen than wheat so I'll put more down. Two pesticide applications should handle the stalk borers and fall armyworm if it shows up.

I'm 62. My back isn't what it was. I'm not going to experiment with new crops or techniques. This rotation works, the buyers are there, and I know it in my bones.
